name: Femi Chen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Femi. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we don't sell anything. Everything you say is confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I put up timber-frame houses for Brookfield Homes, on a new estate called Larkspur Meadow at the edge of town. The wall panels come off a lorry already made in a factory, and we stand them up, fix them, do the floor joists and the roof cassettes, then the first-fix carpentry inside. I start at half seven, and if it's raining the whole estate turns to mud and everything takes twice as long. What I like is when a family drives past on a Sunday to look at their house going up, and you can see on their faces it's the biggest thing they'll ever buy.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who's around you at work, and what's home like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: There's four of us on my gang. Sorin is Romanian and his English is still coming along, so sometimes I use the translate thing on my phone, or ask the AI app to explain a building rule in plain words for both of us. At home it's me and Mei, she works in the dispensary at a pharmacy, and our two girls are grown and gone. We've got three years left on the mortgage, which is the finish line I keep my eye on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So it stays a gadget. That's more or less what I'd expect for building, anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, now let's talk about the things that actually matter on site, like pay and safety. I'm not one for posting, but I'd say it in the cabin over tea. Most of the lads would just shrug.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it means my plan holds. Pay off the house in three years, work till sixty-five or so, then do up the shed and grow tomatoes. The thing that would hurt me is a housing slump, not AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Exactly what I'm doing now. Keep at Brookfield, keep overpaying the mortgage by a bit when there's overtime, and keep using the phone for translating with Sorin, because that does help. Maybe I'd look at whether the union could get the older ones off the roof work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine. Steady. Like a level that reads true.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a housing slump would hurt more. Why that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've lived through one. In 2009 I was out of work for five months and we lived on Mei's wages and beans. Builders stop building the moment people stop buying, and no computer changes that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the AI on your phone, would you use it more if it stayed like this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, for the boring things. It's good at explaining the regulations, the ones written so nobody can read them. But I'd never let it tell me how to fix a joist hanger, I can see that with my own eyes.

S0.say: Good, now let's get back to what matters on site, like pay and safety. I'd say that over tea in the cabin rather than posting anything online.
S0.think: My plan holds: pay off the house in three years, work till about sixty-five, then do up the shed. A housing slump scares me more than AI ever would.
S0.do: Keeps working at Brookfield and overpays the mortgage when there's overtime. Keeps using the phone to translate with Sorin and asks the union about moving older workers off roof work.
S0.feel: Fine and steady, like a level that reads true.
S0.quote: In 2009 I was out of work for five months and we lived on Mei's wages and beans.
S0.fieldNote: His reference point for disaster is the 2009 slump, not technology. He already uses AI for small, practical things like translating for a workmate. The mortgage end date organises his whole plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Strong change but people still working. I think we're already living the start of that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's coming whether we like it or not, so the union had better be at the table for it. More of the house is going to be built in the factory and less on the estate, that's obvious already. I'd say we need training paid for by the firms, not by us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it means fewer of us on site and more in the panel factory over in Ashby. That's not the end of the world. It's dry in there, which at fifty-eight is not nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Brookfield or the panel firm offered training on the factory machines, I'd take it, once I'd seen a couple of the others try it first. I'd keep my head down at work and keep paying off the mortgage. And I'd go to the union meeting on it, which I don't always do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, but not frightened. Change I can see coming, I can deal with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait for others to try it first. Who would you be watching?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Danny from the next gang, he's forty and always first with anything new. If he went to the factory and came back saying it's decent money and you don't get treated like a number, I'd go. If he hated it, I'd stay in the mud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your daughters about this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lin does graphic design in the city, and I'd worry for her more than me. That's exactly the kind of thing these programs do now. I'd tell her to keep her clients close and learn the tools before they learn her job.

S1.say: It's coming whether we like it or not, so the union had better be at the table. More of the house will be built in the factory, and the firms should pay for the training, not us.
S1.think: I think it means fewer of us on site and more in the panel factory over in Ashby. That's not the end of the world, and it's dry in there, which at fifty-eight matters.
S1.do: Takes training on factory machines if offered, after watching a colleague try it first. Keeps paying down the mortgage and goes to the union meeting on the changes.
S1.feel: A bit uneasy but not frightened, because he can see it coming.
S1.quote: If he hated it, I'd stay in the mud.
S1.fieldNote: A classic follower of proof: he names the exact colleague whose verdict would decide him. His concern for his designer daughter outweighs concern for himself. He sees factory work as a possible comfort at his age.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's fast. Faster than Brookfield changes the paint colour in the show home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government needs to step in, now, before it's too late: something for workers, a wage while people adjust, rules on how fast firms can lay people off. I'd sign whatever petition the union put round and I'd go to the march. I'd say it on the estate too, even to the site manager.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, part of me doesn't believe a robot will be standing panels on Larkspur Meadow in the rain by 2028. Making the robot and getting it onto a muddy estate are two different things. But I'd be sixty, the mortgage wouldn't be quite done, and Mei's pharmacy work is exactly the kind of thing AI could swallow, so we'd both be in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd throw every spare penny at the mortgage so we could clear it before anything happens. We'd cut the eating out and put off the new kitchen we've been talking about. I'd go to the union about redundancy terms and push for a government scheme, and I'd sit Lin down about her plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicking, because I still half think the robots would be stuck in the car park. But anxious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Mei's job is exposed too. What would happen at home if you both lost work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the bit that keeps me awake when I think about it. With both of us out, our four months of savings would go in four months, maybe five if we're careful. We'd have to ask the girls for help, which I'd hate, or rely on whatever the government did.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only two years, what would you do in the very first week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ring the bank and ask what it would take to pay off the house early. And talk to Mei properly, at the table, with a pen. We're good at that, we did it in 2009.

S2.say: The government needs to step in now, with a wage while people adjust and rules on how fast firms can lay people off. I'd sign the union petition, go on the march and say it to the site manager.
S2.think: Part of me doesn't believe a robot will be standing panels on a muddy estate by 2028. But I'd be sixty with the mortgage not quite done, and Mei's pharmacy job could go too.
S2.do: Puts every spare penny into clearing the mortgage and cuts eating out and the planned kitchen. Pushes the union for redundancy terms and a government scheme, and talks to his daughter Lin about her plans.
S2.feel: Anxious but not panicking, because he half thinks the robots would get stuck in the car park.
S2.quote: Making the robot and getting it onto a muddy estate are two different things.
S2.fieldNote: His scepticism about how fast robots reach real sites holds his fear in check. The real threat he sees is both incomes going at once. He'd draw on the habits he and Mei learned in 2009.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. 2031. That's after the mortgage is done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same things, the government needs a plan and the firms need to pay their share. But I'd say it with a bit more patience. Five years is long enough to do it properly if they start now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, this one I could manage. The house would be paid off by 2029, so we'd have two years with no mortgage to save hard. If the robots came at sixty-three, I'd be close enough to retire early on a smaller pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd overpay the mortgage to clear it a bit early, then put the old mortgage money straight into savings. I'd probably start using the AI more, to see what it's actually like, maybe learn to run the planning software the site manager uses. And I'd keep pushing in the union for older workers to get a fair exit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, more than anything. There's room to move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd learn the planning software. Is that something you'd really do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Danny had already done it, yes. I'm not going to be the first. But if someone showed me on a wet Tuesday, I'd sit down and learn it, I'm not stupid, I just like to see it works first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes most for you between two years and five?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The house. Two years, we're still paying the bank when it hits. Five years, the house is ours and nobody can take that. Everything else is a worry, but the roof over our heads is the thing.

S3.say: The government needs a plan and the firms need to pay their share. Five years is long enough to do it properly, if they start now.
S3.think: This one I could manage. The house would be paid off by 2029, giving us two years of saving hard, and at sixty-three I could retire early on a smaller pension.
S3.do: Overpays to clear the mortgage early, then saves the freed-up money each month. Learns the site manager's planning software once a colleague has gone first, and pushes in the union for a fair exit for older workers.
S3.feel: Mostly uneasy, with room to move.
S3.quote: Five years, the house is ours and nobody can take that.
S3.fieldNote: The mortgage end date is what separates this scenario from the two-year one for him. He becomes willing to learn new software, though still only after a colleague. His tone shifts from urgent to patient.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2036. I'd be sixty-eight and growing tomatoes, I hope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got ten years to make it fair, so no excuses. Every party should have to say what they'd do about it before the next election. I'd tell that to anyone who asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it hardly touches me. I'd retire around sixty-five like I always planned. The worry would all be for Lin and for Sorin and the younger ones on the gang.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going at Brookfield like normal, finish the mortgage, retire on time. I'd vote for whoever had a real plan for workers. Maybe I'd help train some of the younger ones in how to work with the new machines, if the firm asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit sorry for the young ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Sorin in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him he's thirty-two and he's got time, so learn whatever runs the robots. And learn English properly, because whoever explains things to the customer will last longest. I'd tell him that kindly, he works harder than any of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything you'd find hopeful in it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it means nobody has to be out in January on a roof in sleet, that's not all bad. I've done that for forty years. As long as the people who used to do it get looked after.

S4.say: We've got ten years to make it fair, so there are no excuses. Every party should have to say what they'd do about it before the next election.
S4.think: For me it hardly matters, I'd retire around sixty-five like I always planned. My worry would be for Lin, Sorin and the younger ones on the gang.
S4.do: Carries on at Brookfield, finishes the mortgage and retires on schedule. Votes for whoever has a real plan for workers and helps train younger colleagues on new machines if asked.
S4.feel: Mostly calm, a bit sorry for the young ones.
S4.quote: If it means nobody has to be out in January on a roof in sleet, that's not all bad.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, his own position is secure and his concern turns outward to his daughter and his younger workmate. He sees a real benefit in ending miserable winter roof work. He still insists the displaced must be looked after.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it lands while we're still paying the bank and Mei's job could go at the same time as mine. What would help is a government wage to carry people over while they adjust, and a rule that the firms making the savings pay into it. And a bit more time, honestly, time is what makes the difference for someone my age.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about Sorin and the lads like him. People who came here to work hard in the trades, and their whole plan is built on being needed. I'd want someone looking out for them. Builders are always the first ones laid off and the last ones thought about.

headlineQuote: Builders are always the first ones laid off and the last ones thought about.
portrait: Femi Chen is a 58-year-old timber-frame carpenter for Brookfield Homes, with three years left on his mortgage and a partner, Mei, who works in a pharmacy dispensary. He uses AI now and then to translate for his Romanian workmate and waits for proof before trying anything new. He is calm if AI stalls and uneasy about factory-built housing under steady change. The two-year AGI picture makes him anxious, held back from alarm by his doubt that robots can handle a muddy estate. Once the mortgage is paid, as in the five- and ten-year pictures, he feels he can manage.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because it comes before the mortgage is paid and could take Mei's job at the same time as his.
whatWouldHelp: A government wage to carry people over while they adjust, paid for by the firms making the savings, and more time.
